claims.text: Au and Cu segregate to the surfaces of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during heating.
Au and Cu segregation is driven by minimization of surface energy rather than by sluggish diffusion.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than the other components of the quinary alloy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the FCC bulk structure of the nanoparticles.
For sub-5 nm particles, surface-energy contributions dominate the Gibbs free energy because of the high surface-to-volume ratio.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu lowers the total energy of the nanoparticles.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
Au and Cu evaporate because their boiling points are relatively low compared with those of Pt, Ni, and Co.
Evaporation of segregated elements leads to particle shrinkage and coalescence.
The mechanism becomes dominant at approximately 600–800 K, when the surface-diffusion activation barrier is overcome.
Initial nanoparticle shape affects the surface-energy gradient and hence the rates of segregation and evaporation.
Icosahedral particles possess higher-energy facets and therefore segregate and evaporate faster than truncated-octahedral particles.
The surface-driven process is not limited by sluggish bulk diffusion.
Heating causes a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and a widening of the particle-size distribution.
Heating reshapes the nanoparticles from elliptical to spherical geometries.
The nanoparticle bulk remains FCC while its composition changes over time.
The proposed mechanism is dominant for particles below 10 nm, whereas bulk sluggish diffusion may dominate in larger particles.
